title: Planning a Traditional and White Wedding in Nigeria
excerpt: Organising traditional and white wedding ceremonies? Learn what to decide first, how to coordinate families and dates, and which plans need separate budgets.
author: Ariya Journal
content:
Introduction

Planning a traditional wedding and a white wedding in Nigeria can feel like organising two major events at the same time.

There are family discussions, customary requirements, venues, guest lists, outfits, caterers, photographers, decorators, invitations and several other decisions to coordinate.

The challenge is not simply finding vendors. It is knowing what to organise first, what can be planned together and what must be handled separately.

For example, booking a reception venue before confirming the traditional and white wedding dates could create unnecessary complications. Choosing outfits before understanding the ceremony arrangements may also lead to avoidable expenses.

The best approach is to treat the ceremonies as connected but separate projects.

Your traditional wedding has its own family discussions, customs, requirements and programme. Your white wedding has its own ceremony arrangements, venue, guest experience and vendors. Some resources can be shared, but each event needs a clear plan.

This guide explains how to organise both ceremonies in a practical order, from the first family conversation to the final wedding-day arrangements.

One important principle: Nigerian marriage customs are not identical across ethnic groups, towns, religions or families. Confirm the requirements with the families and relevant religious or marriage authorities rather than assuming that one checklist applies to everyone.

1. Understand the difference between the traditional and white wedding

Before you start booking anything, establish what each ceremony means to your families and what you intend to organise.

Traditional wedding

The traditional wedding is the ceremony through which the couple and their families observe the marriage customs applicable to them.

Depending on the community and family, it may involve:

  • Formal family introductions.
  • Engagement negotiations.
  • Presentation of customary items.
  • Bride-price or other agreed marriage requirements.
  • Family representatives.
  • Traditional outfits.
  • Cultural music and performances.
  • Family prayers, blessings or other rites.
  • A reception or celebration.

The exact structure varies. Even families from the same ethnic group may follow different procedures.

For example, Yoruba engagement ceremonies may involve an engagement list and an alága, while Igbo marriage customs may include family visits, discussions and the igba nkwu ceremony. Hausa Muslim marriage arrangements may centre on the nikah and related family and religious requirements. These are broad descriptions, not universal rules.

White wedding

In Nigeria, the expression white wedding commonly refers to a Christian wedding ceremony, often followed by a reception.

It may involve:

  • Church or other approved ceremony arrangements.
  • Marriage preparation or counselling required by the institution.
  • Wedding attire.
  • Bridesmaids and groomsmen.
  • Rings.
  • Photography and videography.
  • Reception venue.
  • Catering.
  • Decoration.
  • Music and entertainment.
  • Guest invitations and attendance management.

If your ceremony is not Christian, you may have a different religious or civil arrangement. Plan according to the actual ceremony you intend to hold.

Are both ceremonies compulsory?

There is no universal requirement that every Nigerian couple must hold both a traditional and a white wedding.

Couples should distinguish between:

  • Customary marriage requirements applicable to their families and community.
  • Religious ceremonies and requirements.
  • Civil or statutory marriage requirements.

If you want a marriage recognised under the Marriage Act, confirm the current legal process directly with the appropriate marriage registry or a qualified legal professional. Do not assume that every church ceremony automatically completes statutory registration.

2. What should you organise first?

The first step is not choosing wedding colours, booking a decorator or shopping for outfits.

It is getting the important decisions agreed.

Use this order:

  1. Couple's expectations: agree on the wedding you both want.
  2. Family discussions: clarify customary requirements and family expectations early.
  3. Ceremony structure: establish which ceremonies you are holding and how they relate.
  4. Budget and contributions: understand what can realistically be funded.
  5. Dates and locations: these determine venue availability and logistics.
  6. Guest estimates: guest numbers influence venues, catering and other costs.
  7. Major bookings: secure venues and essential vendors.
  8. Ceremony-specific details: plan outfits, engagement items, programme and styling.
  9. Invitations and communication: give guests reliable information.
  10. Final coordination: confirm every person, payment and responsibility.

The order may need to change slightly depending on your circumstances. For instance, a family may need to complete an introduction before agreeing on a traditional wedding date.

The principle is to settle decisions that affect other decisions before committing money.

3. Start with a conversation between the couple

Before bringing everyone into the planning process, the two of you should discuss what you want.

This helps prevent a situation where both families begin making arrangements based on different expectations.

Discuss the following:

The ceremonies

  • Are you holding both traditional and white weddings?
  • Will there also be a registry or civil ceremony?
  • Are you planning a religious ceremony?
  • Will the ceremonies happen on the same day or on separate dates?

The scale

  • Do you want an intimate celebration?
  • Are you expecting a large family gathering?
  • Will you have separate receptions?
  • How many guests do you realistically want to host?

The location

  • Will the traditional wedding take place in the bride's hometown?
  • Will the white wedding take place where you currently live?
  • Will guests need to travel between cities?
  • Will you need accommodation for family members?

Your priorities

  • Is family participation especially important?
  • Is the traditional ceremony the main celebration?
  • Do you want a large white wedding reception?
  • Are photography, food, entertainment or decoration major priorities?

Write down your decisions.

You do not need to have every detail resolved at this stage. You need enough agreement to begin the family discussions confidently.

4. Bring both families into the conversation early

Nigerian weddings can involve significant family participation. This is particularly important when planning a traditional wedding.

Do not leave the first meaningful family discussion until after you have already paid for venues and vendors.

The families should have an opportunity to clarify:

  • The appropriate marriage introduction process.
  • Customary requirements.
  • Engagement or marriage lists, where applicable.
  • Expected family representatives.
  • The role of elders.
  • Ceremony dates and preferred locations.
  • Who will coordinate the family discussions.
  • Any family-specific expectations.

What should the families agree on?

At a minimum, try to establish:

  1. The order of family visits and ceremonies.
  2. Whether a formal introduction is required before the traditional wedding.
  3. The requirements and timing for the traditional ceremony.
  4. Who will communicate official family decisions.
  5. The expected guest numbers.
  6. Whether the families are contributing financially or providing specific items.
  7. Any important cultural or religious restrictions.

Avoid making assumptions about who pays

It is common to hear broad statements about which family is responsible for particular wedding expenses.

However, actual arrangements differ by culture, family and personal agreement.

Some families follow customary expectations closely. Others divide costs between the couple and both families.

Rather than relying on general assumptions, create a clear list of agreed responsibilities.

  • Traditional marriage requirements: assign a responsible person or family and agree on a deadline.
  • Traditional ceremony venue: assign a responsible person or family and agree on a deadline.
  • White wedding ceremony arrangements: assign a responsible person or family and agree on a deadline.
  • Reception catering: assign a responsible person or family and agree on a deadline.
  • Couple's outfits: assign a responsible person or family and agree on a deadline.
  • Guest transportation: assign a responsible person or family and agree on a deadline.

This is not intended to override cultural expectations. It simply makes agreed responsibilities easier to track.

5. Decide whether the traditional and white weddings will be on the same day

This is one of the most important decisions because it affects almost everything else.

There are three common approaches.

Option A: Hold both ceremonies on the same day

Some couples hold their traditional wedding in the morning and their white wedding later in the day.

Potential advantages:

  • Guests may only need to travel once.
  • Some vendor services may be shared.
  • The couple can complete both celebrations within one day.
  • It may reduce the number of separate event dates to coordinate.

Potential challenges:

  • The schedule can become demanding.
  • Outfit changes take time.
  • Family ceremonies may take longer than expected.
  • The venues may be far apart.
  • The same vendors may need to move between locations.
  • Delays in the first ceremony can affect the second.

If you choose this arrangement, build a realistic transition period into the schedule.

Do not assume that a traditional ceremony will finish exactly at the planned time.

You will need to account for:

  • Family introductions and proceedings.
  • Photographs.
  • Travel between venues.
  • Makeup and outfit changes.
  • Guest movement.
  • Venue setup.
  • Vendor access and equipment transfer.

A same-day arrangement is most practical when the locations are close enough and the programme has been properly coordinated.

Option B: Hold the ceremonies on different days

For example, you could hold the traditional wedding on Saturday and the white wedding the following Saturday.

Potential advantages:

  • Each ceremony has its own dedicated time.
  • Family members can focus on the relevant event.
  • There is more flexibility for photographs and outfit changes.
  • Vendors can prepare separately.
  • The couple has more time to recover between events.

Potential challenges:

  • You may pay for separate venue and vendor arrangements.
  • Guests may need to travel more than once.
  • Family members may need additional accommodation.
  • The overall planning period may become longer.

Option C: Hold the ceremonies several weeks or months apart

This arrangement may be suitable when:

  • Families live in different locations.
  • The couple is coordinating from abroad.
  • There are financial reasons to spread expenses.
  • The traditional wedding requires extensive preparation.
  • The white wedding venue or religious institution has limited availability.

It can provide more planning time, but you must manage the two events as parts of one overall wedding plan.

How should you choose?

Consider the following:

  • Guest convenience: same-day events may be easier if locations are close; separate dates may mean guests attend twice.
  • Planning pressure: a same-day celebration is busier; separate dates spread the work.
  • Vendor coordination: shared teams make a same-day event more complex; separate dates are easier to separate.
  • Budget management: a same-day event may share some services; separate dates may involve more event expenses.
  • Family flexibility: a single day leaves less time for each ceremony; separate dates allow more time.
  • Travel requirements: the impact depends heavily on venue locations.

There is no universally better choice. Select the format that fits your families, budget, location and preferred experience.

6. Set your dates and locations

Once the family discussions and ceremony structure are sufficiently clear, agree on the dates.

Do not announce dates publicly until you have checked the most important arrangements.

Questions to answer

  • Which city will host the traditional wedding?
  • Which city will host the white wedding?
  • Are the ceremonies taking place at the same venue?
  • Are they on the same day?
  • Is the venue available?
  • Is the religious institution available?
  • Will important family members be able to attend?
  • Will guests need accommodation?
  • Is the date practical for your major vendors?

Think about travel and logistics

A traditional wedding in the bride's hometown and a white wedding in Lagos, for example, require a different plan from two ceremonies in the same neighbourhood.

Consider:

  • Travel time.
  • Road conditions.
  • Flight availability where relevant.
  • Accommodation.
  • Transportation for older relatives.
  • Movement of wedding outfits and ceremonial items.
  • Vendor transportation.
  • Delivery and storage of equipment.

Avoid scheduling ceremonies so closely that a delay or transport problem at one event makes the next impossible to manage.

7. Create two budgets under one overall wedding budget

Although the ceremonies are connected, track their expenses separately.

Your overall wedding budget should contain three sections:

  1. Traditional wedding.
  2. White wedding.
  3. Shared expenses.

Traditional wedding expenses may include:

  • Engagement requirements.
  • Family gifts.
  • Traditional ceremony venue.
  • Traditional outfits.
  • Catering and drinks.
  • Decoration.
  • Photography and videography.
  • Traditional entertainment.
  • Family logistics.
  • Ceremony coordination.

White wedding expenses may include:

  • Religious or civil ceremony arrangements.
  • Wedding attire.
  • Rings.
  • Reception venue.
  • Catering and drinks.
  • Decoration.
  • Photography and videography.
  • DJ or live band.
  • Cake.
  • Bridal party outfits.
  • Transportation.
  • Guest accommodation.

Shared expenses may include:

  • Wedding planner.
  • Some photography or videography packages.
  • Transportation arrangements.
  • Guest communication.
  • Certain accommodation arrangements.
  • Some administrative and coordination costs.

A vendor may offer a combined package, but check that the package covers both events and does not introduce additional costs through travel, equipment or extra hours.

For a detailed explanation of how to allocate your overall spending, see Ariya's proposed supporting guide: How Much Does a Wedding Cost in Nigeria?

8. Confirm the traditional wedding requirements

Once the family discussions have progressed, obtain the actual requirements for the traditional ceremony.

Do not use a random online engagement list as the final authority.

A list found online may be from a different:

  • Ethnic group.
  • Community.
  • Town.
  • Family.
  • Religious background.

Ask the appropriate family representatives for the requirements that apply to your ceremony.

Create a traditional wedding requirements tracker

  • Family-approved engagement items: confirm the quantity, responsible person, estimated cost and status.
  • Traditional outfits: confirm the quantity, responsible person, estimated cost and status.
  • Drinks and refreshments: confirm the quantity, responsible person, estimated cost and status.
  • Family gifts: confirm the quantity, responsible person, estimated cost and status.
  • Ceremony materials: confirm the quantity, responsible person, estimated cost and status.

Add the actual items once the families have agreed on the list.

Appoint family representatives

It helps to have designated people responsible for communication.

For example:

  • A representative from the bride's family.
  • A representative from the groom's family.
  • A person coordinating the couple's overall plans.
  • A ceremony coordinator familiar with the relevant customs.

This reduces the likelihood of conflicting instructions and repeated discussions.

9. Book the most important venues and vendors

After confirming your dates, guest estimates and ceremony format, begin booking the services that are most important to the successful delivery of the events.

Prioritise the major bookings

Venues

Check availability, capacity, access, power, security, parking, setup restrictions and additional charges.

Planner or coordinator

If you are hiring a planner, clarify whether they are managing both ceremonies or only one.

Photography and videography

Confirm whether the team is available for both dates and what the package includes.

Catering

Obtain separate quotations for the expected guest count at each event.

Decoration

Make sure the decorator understands the different requirements and visual styles of the ceremonies.

Entertainment

Confirm the DJ, MC, live band or cultural performers required for each programme.

Use a vendor comparison sheet

  • Traditional venue: record the quotation, included services, deposit, balance and status.
  • White wedding venue: record the quotation, included services, deposit, balance and status.
  • Photographer for both ceremonies: record the quotation, deliverables, deposit, balance and status.
  • Traditional caterer: record the quotation, menu, deposit, balance and status.
  • White wedding caterer: record the quotation, menu, deposit, balance and status.

Do not book based on a social media post alone. Check the vendor's portfolio, references, written terms, deliverables and payment arrangements.

10. Plan the outfits and Aso-Ebi arrangements

Outfits are an important part of many Nigerian wedding celebrations.

However, the traditional and white wedding may have different clothing requirements.

Traditional wedding outfits

Depending on your family and ceremony, you may need:

  • Traditional attire for the bride.
  • Traditional attire for the groom.
  • Headwear and accessories.
  • Jewellery or beads.
  • Family outfits.
  • Aso-Ebi fabrics.
  • Tailoring and fittings.

White wedding outfits

Possible requirements include:

  • Wedding gown.
  • Groom's suit or formal attire.
  • Bridal party dresses.
  • Groomsmen's outfits.
  • Shoes and accessories.
  • Veil and other bridal accessories.
  • Outfit alterations.

Organise Aso-Ebi early

If you intend to have Aso-Ebi, establish:

  • The selected fabric.
  • The people who will wear it.
  • The price.
  • Who will distribute it.
  • Payment deadlines.
  • Tailoring arrangements.
  • Delivery dates.

Avoid making fabric arrangements without considering the number of people involved and the time required for distribution and tailoring.

11. Manage the guest lists separately

A couple may have different guest lists for the traditional and white wedding.

Some guests may attend both ceremonies, while others may only be invited to one.

Create separate attendance records.

Traditional wedding guest list

Consider:

  • Immediate family.
  • Extended family.
  • Family friends.
  • Community representatives.
  • Traditional ceremony participants.
  • Friends of the couple.

White wedding guest list

Consider:

  • Immediate family.
  • Friends.
  • Colleagues.
  • Church or religious community.
  • Professional contacts.
  • Other invited guests.

Why separate guest lists matter

You may have:

  • Different venue capacities.
  • Different catering arrangements.
  • Different seating requirements.
  • Different invitation messages.
  • Different transportation needs.

Keep one master contact list where appropriate, but maintain separate invitation and attendance statuses for each ceremony.

12. Plan the invitations and guest communication

Do not send invitations until the essential event details are confirmed.

For each ceremony, establish:

  • Date.
  • Time.
  • Venue.
  • Location directions.
  • Dress code.
  • RSVP instructions.
  • Contact for enquiries.
  • Any additional information guests need.

If you are holding both ceremonies, make it clear whether an invitation is for:

  • The traditional wedding only.
  • The white wedding only.
  • Both ceremonies.

Digital invitations can help distribute event information and communicate updates. Printed invitations may still be appropriate for some family members and formal recipients.

For couples managing a large guest list, a clear RSVP process can help estimate attendance and plan catering more accurately.

13. Coordinate the legal and religious arrangements

The traditional ceremony, religious ceremony and statutory marriage process should not be treated as interchangeable.

If you intend to marry under the Marriage Act, confirm the current requirements with the appropriate marriage registry.

If you are having a church or other religious ceremony, speak directly with the institution about:

  • Required documents.
  • Marriage preparation.
  • Counselling.
  • Ceremony scheduling.
  • Witness requirements.
  • Administrative procedures.
  • Any relevant registration process.

Do this early enough to resolve documentation or scheduling issues.

This article is a planning guide, not legal advice. Requirements can depend on the marriage type and the relevant institution.

14. Create separate programmes for the two ceremonies

Each ceremony needs its own programme.

The traditional wedding may involve family representatives and customary proceedings that do not apply to the white wedding.

The white wedding may involve a religious service, procession, vows and reception programme.

Traditional wedding programme

The order must be agreed with the families and the people responsible for the ceremony.

Possible elements include:

  • Guest arrival.
  • Family arrival.
  • Opening prayer or welcome.
  • Introduction of the families.
  • Presentation of customary items.
  • Relevant marriage proceedings.
  • Bride and groom's participation.
  • Family blessings.
  • Couple's celebration.
  • Photographs.
  • Food and entertainment.

The exact order should follow the applicable customs.

White wedding programme

A programme may include:

  • Guest arrival.
  • Seating.
  • Processional.
  • Religious ceremony.
  • Signing or other required formalities.
  • Recessional.
  • Couple's photographs.
  • Reception entrance.
  • Welcome address.
  • Speeches.
  • Meal service.
  • Cake cutting.
  • First dance, where applicable.
  • Entertainment.
  • Closing.

Make sure the programme is shared with the relevant vendors and coordinators.

15. Create one master timeline and two event-day schedules

This is particularly important when the ceremonies are on different dates or share vendors.

Your master timeline should cover the entire planning process.

Your event-day schedules should contain the detailed running order for each ceremony.

Example master planning timeline

  1. 12–9 months before: couple's decisions, family discussions, ceremony format, budget, dates and locations.
  2. 9–6 months before: venue bookings, planner, major vendors and traditional requirements.
  3. 6–4 months before: outfits, Aso-Ebi, guest estimates, photography, decoration and entertainment.
  4. 4–3 months before: invitations, guest communication and legal or religious arrangements.
  5. 3–2 months before: traditional items, programme details, transport and accommodation.
  6. 2–1 month before: vendor confirmations, outfit fittings, final guest numbers and seating.
  7. Final 2 weeks: payment checks, delivery checks, event-day schedules and family briefings.
  8. Final week: confirm responsibilities, contacts, timings and emergency arrangements.

Adjust the timeline to suit your actual engagement and ceremony dates. Some family or legal processes may require a different lead time.

Example same-day schedule

This is an illustrative schedule, not a standard programme. Adapt it to the actual ceremony requirements and travel distances.

  • 6:00 am: couple and key team begin preparation.
  • 8:00 am: vendors complete initial setup.
  • 9:00 am: guests begin arriving.
  • 10:00 am: traditional ceremony begins.
  • 12:30 pm: traditional ceremony and photographs conclude.
  • 12:30?2:00 pm: travel, outfit change and transition.
  • 2:00 pm: white wedding ceremony.
  • 3:30 pm: reception begins.
  • 4:00 pm: meal service and reception programme.
  • 7:00 pm: closing activities.

Do not use this timetable without checking the religious institution's schedule, family programme, venue access and travel time.

16. Assign clear responsibilities

One person should not be expected to manage every detail of two wedding ceremonies.

Create a small coordination structure.

  • Couple: approves major decisions and spending.
  • Bride's family representative: coordinates communication and agreed family responsibilities.
  • Groom's family representative: coordinates communication and agreed family responsibilities.
  • Overall planner: oversees the combined wedding plan.
  • Traditional ceremony coordinator: coordinates traditional ceremony proceedings.
  • White wedding coordinator: coordinates the religious ceremony and reception.
  • Vendor coordinator: confirms vendor arrival, setup and deliverables.
  • Guest coordinator: handles guest questions and attendance.
  • Logistics coordinator: manages transport, accommodation and equipment movement.

Some roles can be combined, depending on the size of the events.

The important thing is that every major responsibility has a named person.

17. Common mistakes when planning both ceremonies

1. Booking vendors before agreeing on the dates

This can create unnecessary cancellation costs and scheduling problems.

2. Treating both ceremonies as one event

They may share vendors and resources, but their programmes, guest lists and requirements are different.

3. Assuming all families follow the same customs

Confirm requirements directly with the families involved.

4. Failing to agree on family responsibilities

Unclear responsibilities can lead to disagreement, duplicated spending and last-minute pressure.

5. Choosing the same-day option without calculating transition time

A tight schedule can create delays and affect the experience of both ceremonies.

6. Combining all expenses into one untracked budget

Separate traditional, white wedding and shared expenses.

7. Forgetting guests who need to travel

Consider accommodation, transport and the time required to move between locations.

8. Leaving legal and religious requirements too late

Contact the relevant institution early and confirm its current process.

9. Giving too many people authority to change the programme

Agree on who can approve changes and who communicates instructions to vendors.

10. Failing to prepare one final coordination document

Everyone involved should have access to the final timetable, venue details and relevant contact information.

18. Traditional and white wedding planning checklist

Stage 1: Couple's decisions

  • Agree on the overall wedding vision.
  • Decide which ceremonies you intend to hold.
  • Decide whether the ceremonies will be on the same day.
  • Discuss preferred locations.
  • Agree on a realistic guest estimate.
  • Establish the available budget.

Stage 2: Family discussions

  • Arrange the appropriate family introduction.
  • Identify family representatives.
  • Confirm traditional marriage requirements.
  • Discuss expected family responsibilities.
  • Agree on the preferred ceremony dates.
  • Clarify who will coordinate family communication.

Stage 3: Dates, venues and vendors

  • Confirm the dates.
  • Check venue availability.
  • Confirm religious or registry arrangements.
  • Decide whether to hire a wedding planner.
  • Book essential vendors.
  • Review contracts and payment schedules.
  • Confirm vendor availability for both ceremonies.

Stage 4: Traditional wedding arrangements

  • Confirm the engagement list or applicable requirements.
  • Assign responsibility for each item.
  • Arrange traditional outfits.
  • Confirm Aso-Ebi arrangements.
  • Plan catering and drinks.
  • Confirm the traditional ceremony programme.
  • Arrange family logistics.

Stage 5: White wedding arrangements

  • Confirm the ceremony institution and requirements.
  • Select the wedding outfits.
  • Arrange rings.
  • Confirm the bridal party.
  • Book reception catering.
  • Finalise decoration.
  • Confirm photography and videography.
  • Plan the reception programme.

Stage 6: Guests and communication

  • Create separate guest lists.
  • Confirm invitation details.
  • Send invitations.
  • Establish RSVP deadlines.
  • Arrange transportation where required.
  • Confirm accommodation for travelling guests.
  • Communicate any changes promptly.

Stage 7: Final coordination

  • Confirm all vendors.
  • Confirm payment balances.
  • Complete outfit fittings.
  • Check traditional ceremony items.
  • Finalise both event-day programmes.
  • Share contact lists with coordinators.
  • Confirm venue setup and access.
  • Prepare an emergency plan.
  • Protect time for the couple to rest and enjoy the celebrations.

19. How Ariya can support your wedding planning

When you are planning two ceremonies, information can quickly become scattered across WhatsApp conversations, spreadsheets, emails and family discussions.

A clear digital event-planning process can make it easier to communicate event details and keep guest information organised.

  • Ceremony-specific guest lists.
  • Shared and separate vendor details.
  • Event-specific budgets.

  • Separate event-day schedules.

Frequently asked questions

1. Should the traditional wedding come before the white wedding?

The order depends on the couple's circumstances, family customs and the type of marriage ceremonies being organised. Many couples hold the traditional ceremony before the white wedding, but you should confirm the appropriate sequence with both families and the relevant religious or legal authorities.

2. Can a traditional and white wedding be held on the same day in Nigeria?

Yes. Some couples organise both on the same day. However, you need enough time for the ceremonies, photographs, travel, outfit changes and venue transitions. It is especially important to check whether the same vendors are expected to work at both events.

3. How many months should I plan for a traditional and white wedding?

A planning period of around 9–12 months can give many couples time to coordinate family discussions, dates, venues, vendors and outfits. Smaller weddings may require less time, while weddings involving multiple locations or complex family arrangements may need more.

4. Who pays for the traditional and white wedding?

Payment responsibilities vary by family, culture and personal agreement. Discuss the expected contributions early and record who has agreed to pay for each expense. Do not assume that every Nigerian family follows the same financial arrangement.

5. Can the traditional and white wedding have different guest lists?

Yes. You can maintain separate guest lists for each ceremony. This is useful when the traditional wedding is primarily a family event and the white wedding includes colleagues, friends and a wider social circle.

6. Should I hire one wedding planner for both ceremonies?

You can hire one planner to manage both ceremonies if they have the capacity and relevant experience. Make sure the contract clearly identifies which events are included, the services provided, the number of coordinators and any additional charges.

7. Can I use the same photographer for both weddings?

Yes, provided the photographer is available for both dates and the agreed package covers the required hours, locations, travel and deliverables. If the ceremonies are on the same day, confirm how the team will manage the transition.

8. How do I manage traditional wedding requirements?

Obtain the requirements directly from the appropriate family representatives. Record each item, its quantity, who is responsible and when it must be delivered. Do not rely solely on generic engagement lists found online.

9. Do I need a registry wedding if I am having a traditional and white wedding?

This depends on the legal status and requirements of the marriage you intend to enter. If you want a statutory marriage under the Marriage Act, confirm the process with the appropriate marriage registry or a qualified legal professional. Do not assume that a traditional or religious ceremony automatically completes statutory registration.

10. What if the bride's family lives in another state?

Plan the family visits, traditional ceremony and guest travel around the location. Consider whether the traditional wedding should take place in the bride's hometown, how family members will travel and whether accommodation is needed. Confirm vendor availability in that location before making bookings.

11. What should I book first: the traditional wedding venue or the white wedding venue?

First agree on the ceremony dates, locations and approximate guest counts. Then check availability and book the venues that are most important or likely to be in high demand. You should not book either venue without understanding how the two ceremonies fit together.

12. What is the biggest challenge when planning both ceremonies?

Coordination is often the biggest challenge. You are managing different family expectations, requirements, guest lists, budgets, vendors and schedules. Clear responsibilities, separate event plans and one overall timeline can make the process easier.

Conclusion

Planning a traditional and white wedding in Nigeria becomes easier when you understand that the two ceremonies are connected but not identical.

Start with the couple's expectations, involve both families early, clarify the traditional requirements, agree on dates and locations, and then move on to venues, vendors, outfits and guest communication.

Do not rush into bookings before the decisions that affect them have been settled.

Most importantly, build a plan that respects the families and customs involved while remaining realistic about your time, budget and capacity.

The objective is not simply to organise two beautiful ceremonies. It is to create a well-coordinated celebration that allows both families and the couple to enjoy the occasion.

content:
Introduction

Planning a Nigerian wedding involves more than choosing a date, booking a venue and sending invitations.

You may need to coordinate family introductions, traditional marriage requirements, a white wedding or religious ceremony, guest lists, Aso-Ebi, vendors, catering, outfits, transportation and several other details.

When these responsibilities are not organised properly, it becomes easy to forget important tasks, make rushed decisions or spend money on arrangements that later need to change.

A wedding planning checklist helps you know what to do, when to do it and who is responsible.

This guide provides a practical month-by-month Nigerian wedding planning checklist, starting 12 months before the wedding and continuing through the final week and after the celebration.

It covers both traditional and white wedding arrangements, with adjustments for couples planning only one ceremony or working with a shorter timeline.

Before you begin: Every wedding is different. Some couples have a traditional wedding and white wedding on separate dates, while others combine ceremonies or organise a registry or religious ceremony separately. Nigerian customs also differ between communities and families. Adapt this checklist to your actual requirements rather than treating every item as compulsory.

1. Your Nigerian wedding checklist at a glance

Here is the overall planning sequence.

  1. 12 months before: agree on the wedding vision, budget, family expectations, guest estimate and preferred dates.
  2. 11 months before: confirm ceremony format, family discussions, locations and venue research.
  3. 10 months before: confirm dates, secure venues and begin major vendor bookings.
  4. 9 months before: book photography, videography, planning support and other priority vendors.
  5. 8 months before: develop the traditional wedding plan, outfits and Aso-Ebi arrangements.
  6. 7 months before: work on guest lists, catering, entertainment and decoration.
  7. 6 months before: confirm major design decisions, traditional requirements and vendor contracts.
  8. 5 months before: progress invitations, outfits, transportation and accommodation.
  9. 4 months before: confirm guest communication, programmes and outstanding vendor decisions.
  10. 3 months before: review bookings, complete important purchases and begin detailed coordination.
  11. 2 months before: confirm guest numbers, outfits, logistics and ceremony arrangements.
  12. 1 month before: finalise vendors, payments, programmes and operational details.
  13. 2 weeks before: reconfirm important arrangements and resolve outstanding issues.
  14. 1 week before: complete final checks, pack essentials and brief the wedding team.
  15. Wedding day: follow the programme, coordinate vendors and enjoy the celebration.
  16. After the wedding: settle outstanding matters, thank guests and review vendor services.

This is a flexible timeline. A wedding with several ceremonies, multiple locations or extensive family requirements may need more preparation time.

2. 12 months before the wedding: Establish the foundation

The first stage is about making decisions that will influence everything else.

Do not begin with decoration ideas or expensive purchases. Start with the couple's expectations, family discussions and financial capacity.

Couple's decisions

  • Agree on the type of wedding you want.
  • Decide whether you are having a traditional wedding.
  • Decide whether you are having a white wedding or another religious ceremony.
  • Establish whether a registry or civil ceremony is also required.
  • Discuss whether the ceremonies will happen on the same day or separate dates.
  • Decide which city or cities will host the celebrations.
  • Agree on the overall wedding vision.
  • Identify your most important priorities.

Family discussions

  • Inform the relevant family members.
  • Arrange the appropriate introduction or family meeting.
  • Identify family representatives.
  • Discuss customary marriage requirements.
  • Establish the expected family involvement.
  • Discuss possible financial contributions.
  • Identify any important cultural or religious considerations.

Budget and guest estimate

  • Agree on the total available budget.
  • Identify who is contributing financially.
  • Establish an initial guest estimate for each ceremony.
  • Separate traditional wedding and white wedding expenses.
  • Identify shared expenses.
  • Set aside a contingency amount.
  • Create a wedding budget tracker.

Research and planning

  • Research possible venues.
  • Research wedding planners or coordinators.
  • Research photographers and videographers.
  • Create a preliminary vendor list.
  • Start a wedding planning folder.
  • Create a master planning calendar.

Important: Your budget and guest count should influence your venue decisions. Avoid choosing a venue simply because it looks attractive online.

3. 11 months before the wedding: Confirm the ceremony structure

At this stage, the couple and families should begin turning the broad wedding idea into a workable plan.

Ceremony arrangements

  • Confirm which ceremonies you intend to hold.
  • Agree on the preferred sequence of ceremonies.
  • Confirm whether ceremonies will be held on the same day.
  • Identify the preferred dates.
  • Confirm the likely locations.
  • Discuss the traditional ceremony requirements with the relevant family representatives.
  • Contact the relevant religious institution or registry about its procedures.

Venue research

  • Visit suitable venues.
  • Check the venue's capacity.
  • Ask about rental charges.
  • Confirm what furniture and equipment are included.
  • Ask about power supply and generator arrangements.
  • Check ventilation or air-conditioning.
  • Confirm parking and security.
  • Ask about setup and closing times.
  • Check restrictions on external caterers, decorators and other vendors.

Vendor research

  • Shortlist potential planners.
  • Shortlist photographers and videographers.
  • Research caterers.
  • Research decorators.
  • Research DJs, MCs and live bands.
  • Research makeup artists and stylists.
  • Request sample quotations.

4. 10 months before the wedding: Secure your major bookings

Some venues and experienced vendors have limited availability, particularly during busy wedding periods.

Once your dates and requirements are sufficiently clear, secure the services that matter most.

Bookings

  • Confirm the wedding date.
  • Book the traditional wedding venue, if applicable.
  • Book the white wedding or reception venue.
  • Confirm the religious ceremony date and arrangements.
  • Book your wedding planner, if required.
  • Book your photographer.
  • Book your videographer.
  • Review contracts and payment schedules.
  • Record all deposits and outstanding balances.

Planning documents

  • Create a vendor contact list.
  • Create a booking and payment tracker.
  • Record vendor responsibilities.
  • Save copies of contracts and receipts.
  • Record cancellation and rescheduling conditions.

Guest planning

  • Begin the master guest list.
  • Identify important family and community guests.
  • Estimate the number of guests for each ceremony.
  • Identify guests who may need accommodation or transportation.

5. 9 months before the wedding: Develop the wedding experience

Now begin working on the details that will shape how the celebrations look and feel.

Wedding theme and styling

  • Agree on the overall colour direction.
  • Decide on the traditional wedding colour scheme.
  • Decide on the white wedding reception theme.
  • Discuss decoration preferences.
  • Research floral and stage designs.
  • Decide whether you want a specific reception layout.
  • Begin discussing signage and other visual materials.

Traditional wedding planning

  • Obtain the applicable traditional marriage requirements.
  • Identify the person coordinating the traditional ceremony.
  • Discuss the ceremony programme with family representatives.
  • Identify any traditional performers or specialists required.
  • Begin planning traditional attire.
  • Discuss Aso-Ebi arrangements.

White wedding planning

  • Begin researching wedding gowns and suits.
  • Decide whether you will have bridesmaids and groomsmen.
  • Discuss the bridal party arrangements.
  • Research wedding rings.
  • Discuss the reception programme.
  • Begin identifying possible music selections.

Vendor selection

  • Compare photographer and videographer portfolios.
  • Confirm photography coverage requirements.
  • Review decorator proposals.
  • Compare catering quotations.
  • Review entertainment options.
  • Confirm the services included in each quotation.

6. 8 months before the wedding: Confirm outfits and Aso-Ebi arrangements

Outfits can require several fittings, adjustments and delivery arrangements. Do not leave them until the final few weeks.

Couple's outfits

  • Confirm the traditional outfits.
  • Confirm the white wedding attire.
  • Choose fabrics.
  • Select designers or tailors.
  • Confirm measurements and fitting dates.
  • Select shoes and accessories.
  • Discuss outfit changes, if any.
  • Confirm the expected delivery dates.

Bridal party and family outfits

  • Confirm bridesmaids' outfits.
  • Confirm groomsmen's outfits.
  • Discuss family clothing arrangements.
  • Agree on Aso-Ebi colours and fabric.
  • Select the fabric supplier.
  • Establish the ordering and payment process.
  • Decide who will distribute the fabric.

Traditional ceremony

  • Confirm the engagement list or applicable requirements.
  • Assign responsibility for sourcing items.
  • Identify any items that require special preparation.
  • Confirm who will oversee the ceremony proceedings.

7. 7 months before the wedding: Work on guest experience and major services

At this stage, the planning should move beyond the couple and vendors to the people who will attend.

Guest list

  • Review the guest list with both families.
  • Separate traditional and white wedding guests.
  • Remove duplicate entries.
  • Confirm how invitations will be distributed.
  • Identify guests travelling from outside the event city.
  • Begin considering seating arrangements.

Catering

  • Shortlist caterers.
  • Discuss menu options.
  • Request quotations for each ceremony.
  • Consider local dishes and guest preferences.
  • Discuss special dietary requirements.
  • Confirm whether service staff and serving equipment are included.

Entertainment

  • Book your DJ or live band.
  • Book your MC.
  • Confirm traditional performers, where applicable.
  • Discuss sound and lighting requirements.
  • Identify special performances or programme activities.

Other services

  • Research makeup artists.
  • Research hairstylists.
  • Research cake designers.
  • Research transportation providers.
  • Discuss souvenirs.
  • Consider guest accommodation.

8. 6 months before the wedding: Review the major arrangements

Halfway through a 12-month planning period, review what has been completed and what remains outstanding.

Vendor review

  • Confirm all major vendor bookings.
  • Review payment deadlines.
  • Confirm the scope of every vendor contract.
  • Check that the vendors understand the ceremony format.
  • Confirm availability for both dates, if applicable.
  • Review backup arrangements.

Traditional wedding

  • Review the customary requirements.
  • Confirm responsibility for each item.
  • Review the traditional ceremony programme.
  • Confirm the traditional ceremony coordinator.
  • Review outfit progress.
  • Review Aso-Ebi arrangements.

White wedding

  • Confirm the religious ceremony requirements.
  • Review the wedding attire arrangements.
  • Confirm the bridal party.
  • Review reception design.
  • Confirm any necessary documentation.
  • Review the reception programme.

Guest and logistics planning

  • Review the guest list.
  • Confirm likely attendance numbers.
  • Identify accommodation needs.
  • Review transportation requirements.
  • Consider elderly guests and guests with accessibility needs.

9. 5 months before the wedding: Move into detailed coordination

This is the stage where the individual arrangements begin coming together.

Invitations and communication

  • Confirm invitation wording.
  • Confirm event details.
  • Decide which invitations will be printed.
  • Decide which invitations will be digital.
  • Confirm RSVP instructions.
  • Prepare a guest communication plan.

Photography and videography

  • Discuss the photography schedule.
  • Prepare a list of important family photographs.
  • Identify important people who must be photographed.
  • Discuss any special moments to capture.
  • Confirm expected delivery formats.

Styling and decoration

  • Review decoration proposals.
  • Confirm the stage and backdrop design.
  • Discuss guest table arrangements.
  • Review lighting requirements.
  • Confirm signage and welcome areas.
  • Agree on what will be provided by the venue and what the decorator must bring.

Logistics

  • Identify key transportation needs.
  • Research accommodation options.
  • Discuss vendor transportation.
  • Confirm whether the venue has sufficient power capacity.
  • Identify backup power requirements.

10. 4 months before the wedding: Confirm the details guests and vendors need

At this point, your planning should be sufficiently developed for you to communicate reliable information to guests and vendors.

Guest communication

  • Confirm invitation lists.
  • Prepare the invitation designs.
  • Check names and addresses.
  • Confirm event locations.
  • Confirm ceremony start times.
  • Prepare directions and location information.
  • Establish RSVP deadlines.

Traditional ceremony

  • Review the engagement requirements with the families.
  • Confirm the traditional programme.
  • Confirm the people responsible for each part of the ceremony.
  • Review outstanding purchases.
  • Confirm the traditional outfits.

White wedding

  • Review the ceremony programme.
  • Confirm the officiant or religious institution's requirements.
  • Review attire and accessories.
  • Confirm bridal party responsibilities.
  • Review the reception programme.

Financial review

  • Compare estimated costs with agreed vendor prices.
  • Record all payments.
  • Identify outstanding balances.
  • Review the contingency fund.
  • Discuss any proposed changes before approving additional spending.

11. 3 months before the wedding: Complete the important preparations

The final three months should focus on completion, confirmation and coordination rather than major changes.

Invitations and guest management

  • Send invitations according to your distribution plan.
  • Begin tracking responses.
  • Follow up with important guests.
  • Update the guest list.
  • Identify guests who need transport or accommodation.
  • Begin preparing seating arrangements where appropriate.

Outfits and beauty

  • Attend outfit fittings.
  • Confirm final outfit designs.
  • Confirm shoes and accessories.
  • Arrange makeup trials.
  • Arrange hair trials.
  • Confirm the styling schedule.
  • Confirm outfit delivery dates.

Vendors

  • Reconfirm all major vendor bookings.
  • Review delivery timelines.
  • Confirm setup requirements.
  • Confirm arrival times.
  • Confirm remaining payments.
  • Record emergency contact numbers.

Legal and religious arrangements

  • Check outstanding documents.
  • Confirm required appointments.
  • Confirm any counselling or preparation requirements.
  • Confirm the ceremony schedule with the relevant institution.
  • Resolve outstanding administrative issues.

12. 2 months before the wedding: Finalise the guest and event arrangements

Your attention should now move to the details that can directly affect the event day.

Guest management

  • Review RSVP responses.
  • Follow up on outstanding responses.
  • Update the attendance estimate.
  • Confirm guest seating requirements.
  • Confirm transportation arrangements.
  • Confirm accommodation.
  • Identify guests who need special assistance.

Catering and drinks

  • Review the menu with the caterer.
  • Confirm expected guest numbers.
  • Discuss food quantities.
  • Discuss drinks quantities.
  • Confirm service staff.
  • Confirm serving equipment.
  • Discuss food delivery and setup times.

Traditional wedding

  • Confirm the traditional ceremony requirements.
  • Check the progress of all required items.
  • Confirm Aso-Ebi distribution.
  • Confirm family arrival arrangements.
  • Review the ceremony programme.
  • Confirm any outstanding family decisions.

White wedding

  • Confirm the ceremony programme.
  • Confirm the reception programme.
  • Review the seating arrangement.
  • Confirm the music selections.
  • Confirm cake arrangements.
  • Review decoration and lighting.

13. 1 month before the wedding: Lock down the arrangements

This is one of the most important stages.

Avoid making unnecessary changes. Your priority should be ensuring that everyone knows what they are responsible for.

Vendor confirmation

  • Contact every vendor.
  • Confirm dates and locations.
  • Confirm arrival times.
  • Confirm setup and breakdown requirements.
  • Confirm the agreed deliverables.
  • Confirm outstanding balances.
  • Review contracts.
  • Confirm emergency contact details.

Guest confirmation

  • Review the final guest list.
  • Follow up on outstanding RSVPs.
  • Confirm seating arrangements.
  • Confirm guest transportation.
  • Confirm accommodation.
  • Prepare any necessary guest information messages.

Outfits and accessories

  • Complete major outfit fittings.
  • Confirm delivery of outfits.
  • Check shoes and accessories.
  • Confirm the bridal party's outfits.
  • Check Aso-Ebi arrangements.
  • Organise outfit storage and transportation.

Traditional requirements

  • Review the complete engagement list.
  • Confirm that all required items are accounted for.
  • Check quantities.
  • Label and organise items where appropriate.
  • Assign someone to oversee delivery and safekeeping.
  • Confirm family representatives and arrival times.

Event operations

  • Prepare the event-day programme.
  • Confirm the MC's responsibilities.
  • Share the programme with relevant vendors.
  • Confirm venue access.
  • Review power arrangements.
  • Confirm security and parking.
  • Prepare a contingency plan.

14. Two weeks before the wedding: Reconfirm everything

At this point, the focus should be on eliminating uncertainty.

Final vendor checks

  • Reconfirm every vendor.
  • Confirm arrival times.
  • Confirm venue access.
  • Confirm equipment and setup requirements.
  • Confirm transportation and delivery arrangements.
  • Confirm outstanding payments.
  • Share the final contact list.

Guest and family checks

  • Confirm final attendance estimates.
  • Confirm family representatives.
  • Confirm important guest arrangements.
  • Review seating arrangements.
  • Confirm transport and accommodation.
  • Send reminders where necessary.

Personal preparations

  • Confirm final outfit fittings.
  • Collect outfits that are ready.
  • Check jewellery and accessories.
  • Confirm makeup and hairstyling appointments.
  • Pack important personal items.
  • Confirm honeymoon arrangements, if applicable.

Venue checks

  • Visit the venue if possible.
  • Confirm power and backup arrangements.
  • Confirm cooling and ventilation.
  • Check parking and security.
  • Confirm setup times.
  • Review the layout with the coordinator.

15. One week before the wedding: Prepare for execution

Your wedding should now be organised well enough that you are not trying to solve major planning problems.

Final checks

  • Confirm all vendors again.
  • Confirm final guest numbers with the caterer.
  • Confirm food and drinks quantities.
  • Confirm venue setup.
  • Confirm the programme.
  • Confirm transportation.
  • Confirm accommodation.
  • Confirm the wedding party's responsibilities.
  • Check the traditional marriage requirements.
  • Prepare payment records and agreed balances.

Pack a wedding emergency kit

Your kit may include:

  • Safety pins.
  • Needle and thread.
  • Small scissors.
  • Plasters.
  • Tissues.
  • Wet wipes.
  • Hand sanitiser.
  • Deodorant.
  • Makeup touch-up items.
  • Phone chargers.
  • Power bank.
  • Spare phone cable.
  • Water.
  • Basic personal medication, if required.
  • Printed programme.
  • Vendor contact list.
  • Small emergency cash.

Assign the kit to a reliable person rather than carrying it around yourself.

Personal preparations

  • Collect all outfits.
  • Organise accessories.
  • Confirm the beauty schedule.
  • Prepare the clothes for the day before.
  • Confirm travel arrangements.
  • Avoid introducing unnecessary last-minute changes.
  • Get enough rest.

16. The day before the wedding

The day before should be used for final confirmation and rest.

Venue and vendor preparation

  • Confirm that the venue is ready for the planned setup.
  • Confirm that key vendors know their arrival times.
  • Check the sound and power arrangements where possible.
  • Confirm the person supervising the setup.
  • Review the event-day programme.
  • Confirm transportation arrangements.

Couple and family preparation

  • Pack all outfits.
  • Check accessories.
  • Confirm the makeup and hairstyling schedule.
  • Confirm the family's arrival arrangements.
  • Hand over the emergency kit.
  • Ensure ceremonial items are safely stored.
  • Charge phones and power banks.
  • Get adequate rest.

Avoid turning the day before into another full planning day. Your coordinator and assigned team should handle operational checks.

17. Wedding day checklist

The wedding day is for execution, not making major planning decisions.

The couple should have designated people handling vendors, guests, family communication and logistics.

Before the ceremony

  • Wake up according to the preparation schedule.
  • Eat something suitable before getting dressed.
  • Confirm the makeup and hairstyling team has arrived.
  • Confirm outfits and accessories are ready.
  • Confirm the photographer and videographer are present.
  • Confirm the venue setup.
  • Confirm sound and power.
  • Confirm catering and drinks arrangements.
  • Confirm that the coordinator has the final programme.

During the ceremony

  • Follow the agreed programme.
  • Allow the coordinator to manage vendor questions.
  • Ensure the relevant family representatives are present.
  • Keep ceremonial items secure.
  • Complete important family photographs.
  • Keep the couple informed of significant schedule changes.
  • Allow time for meals, water and rest.

During the reception

  • Confirm the MC has the programme.
  • Confirm the DJ or band knows the important music selections.
  • Monitor meal service.
  • Confirm the couple's entrance arrangements.
  • Keep important personal belongings secure.
  • Coordinate transport after the event.

Most importantly, make time to enjoy the celebration.

18. After the wedding: Do not forget the final responsibilities

Planning does not end when the guests leave.

Financial and vendor follow-up

  • Confirm services have been delivered.
  • Review outstanding vendor balances.
  • Settle agreed payments.
  • Collect receipts and payment records.
  • Record any unresolved issues.
  • Request final deliverables from photographers and videographers.

Guest appreciation

  • Thank family members.
  • Send appreciation messages to guests.
  • Thank people who contributed financially or otherwise.
  • Acknowledge vendors who delivered excellent service.
  • Return borrowed items where applicable.

Personal and administrative matters

  • Collect wedding outfits and personal belongings.
  • Confirm storage or preservation arrangements for important items.
  • Follow up on photographs and videos.
  • Complete any outstanding administrative processes.
  • Review your final wedding spending against the original budget.

19. A shorter wedding planning checklist: What if you have only six months?

Not every couple has a full year to prepare.

If you have six months, you can compress the timeline, but you should not skip the decisions that affect everything else.

  • 6 months before: agree on budget, guest count, family requirements, dates and venues.
  • 5 months before: book major vendors, confirm ceremony structure and begin outfit arrangements.
  • 4 months before: confirm catering, decoration, entertainment, traditional requirements and invitations.
  • 3 months before: send invitations, organise transport and accommodation, and progress outfits and programmes.
  • 2 months before: review RSVPs, confirm guest numbers, vendors, traditional items and logistics.
  • 1 month before: complete final fittings, vendor confirmations, payment tracking and event-day schedules.
  • Final 2 weeks: reconfirm important details, pack essentials and brief the coordination team.
  • Wedding day: execute the programme and enjoy the celebration.

For a shorter timeline, make decisions promptly and prioritise availability. You may need to be flexible about dates, venues and vendors.

20. A wedding planning checklist for couples organising from abroad

Planning a Nigerian wedding from another country introduces additional coordination challenges.

You may be communicating with family members, vendors and guests across different time zones.

Use these additional checks:

  • Appoint a reliable local representative.
  • Agree on who can approve spending.
  • Establish a regular planning meeting.
  • Use one shared document for vendor details.
  • Request written quotations.
  • Request evidence of vendor work and references.
  • Confirm payments through reliable channels.
  • Keep digital copies of contracts and receipts.
  • Arrange local venue inspections.
  • Confirm transportation and accommodation.
  • Avoid relying solely on WhatsApp promises for major bookings.
  • Confirm every important arrangement before travelling.
  • Allow time for delays and changes.

If possible, arrange a trusted local person to inspect major services before the event.

21. How to keep your wedding checklist organised

A checklist is only useful if you can see what has been completed, what is outstanding and who is responsible.

Use a simple task-tracking system.

  • Confirm wedding date: 12 months before; couple and families; pending.
  • Book venue: 10 months before; couple; pending.
  • Confirm photographer: 9 months before; couple; pending.
  • Confirm traditional requirements: 8 months before; family representatives; pending.
  • Send invitations: 3 months before; guest coordinator; pending.
  • Confirm final guest numbers: 2 weeks before; guest coordinator; pending.
  • Reconfirm vendors: 1 week before; wedding planner; pending.
  • Not started.
  • In progress.
  • Awaiting confirmation.
  • Completed.
  • Delayed.

Keep these documents together

Create one central wedding planning folder containing:

  1. Wedding budget.
  2. Master guest list.
  3. Traditional wedding requirements.
  4. Vendor contact list.
  5. Vendor contracts.
  6. Payment records.
  7. Invitation details.
  8. RSVP records.
  9. Event-day programme.
  10. Transportation and accommodation details.
  11. Emergency contacts.
  12. Final checklist.

This will reduce the time spent searching through messages and documents.

22. How Ariya can support your wedding planning

A wedding checklist becomes more useful when the couple can also organise the event information and guest communication connected to it.

Ariya provides digital event-planning tools that couples can explore as part of their preparation.

Ariya

A useful future Ariya feature would be a Nigerian wedding planning checklist that allows couples to:

  • Add tasks and deadlines.
  • Assign responsibilities.
  • Track completed and outstanding tasks.
  • Organise traditional and white wedding activities separately.
  • Keep vendor information together.
  • Track guest invitations and responses.
  • Connect planning tasks to event dates.

This is a proposed product opportunity, not a claim that all these functions are currently available.

Frequently asked questions

1. How early should I start planning a Nigerian wedding?

A 9–12-month planning period is a useful starting point for many weddings, particularly when there are multiple ceremonies, large guest numbers or extensive family arrangements. Smaller celebrations may require less time.

2. What is the first thing to do when planning a wedding in Nigeria?

Start by agreeing on the type of wedding, overall budget, approximate guest count, family expectations and preferred location. These decisions influence the venue, vendors and other expenses.

3. What should I book first for a Nigerian wedding?

Once the date and basic requirements are agreed, prioritise the venue and high-demand vendors whose availability could affect your plans. This may include the planner, photographer and videographer.

4. How do I plan a traditional and white wedding together?

Create one overall wedding plan with separate sections for the traditional and white wedding. Track their guest lists, programmes, vendors and expenses separately while identifying services that can be shared.

5. How many months before a wedding should I send invitations?

The timing depends on the type of invitation, guest travel requirements and the complexity of the event. For a wedding with guests travelling from other cities or countries, communicate the date early and send formal invitations once the details are confirmed.

6. When should I buy Aso-Ebi for my wedding?

Start discussing the fabric and colour early enough to allow sourcing, payment, distribution and tailoring. The exact deadline depends on the supplier, number of people involved and complexity of the outfits.

7. What should I include in a Nigerian wedding checklist?

Include family arrangements, budget, dates, venues, vendors, traditional requirements, outfits, guest lists, invitations, catering, transportation, legal or religious arrangements and final event-day coordination.

8. How can I plan a wedding in six months?

Settle the budget, dates, guest count and venue immediately. Book major vendors, confirm family requirements, organise outfits and invitations, and use a weekly task tracker to monitor progress.

9. Do I need a wedding planner?

Not every wedding requires a full-service planner. However, a coordinator can be valuable when you have multiple ceremonies, many vendors, large guest numbers or are planning from abroad. Decide based on the complexity of your event and the support available.

10. How do I avoid forgetting important wedding tasks?

Keep one master checklist, assign every task to a responsible person, set deadlines and review progress regularly. Do not rely entirely on memory or scattered chat messages.

11. What should I do one week before my wedding?

Reconfirm all vendors, final guest numbers, catering, outfits, transport, venue arrangements, payment schedules and the event programme. Pack an emergency kit and make sure the coordination team has the necessary contact information.

12. What should I do after my wedding?

Settle outstanding vendor matters, collect final photographs and videos, thank guests and family members, return borrowed items and review your final spending.

Conclusion

A Nigerian wedding becomes easier to manage when every important task has a clear deadline and a responsible person.

Start with the decisions that affect the entire celebration: your budget, family arrangements, ceremony structure, dates and guest count. Then move to venues, vendors, outfits, invitations and the final operational details.

Do not wait until the last few weeks to organise important requirements.

Use this checklist as a working document, adapt it to your ceremonies and review it regularly. The aim is to reduce last-minute pressure so that you and your families can focus on celebrating the occasion.
